questions.text: Where does the browser usually place rendering relative to microtasks?
options: After the microtask queue is empty and before the next macrotask, when a frame is due
Only after every macrotask in the queue

questions.text: A queueMicrotask scheduled inside setTimeout runs after that timeout callback and before the next timer.
How do ECMAScript job queues relate to the browser event loop queues?
questions.answer: The JS spec defines Jobs and Job Queues (Promise Jobs). The host (browser, Node) decides when to run those jobs against its own work: timers, I/O, rendering. “Microtask vs macrotask” is the host model on top of JS jobs.

questions.text: What does an endless queueMicrotask(() => queueMicrotask(...)) chain do?
options: It starves macrotasks and rendering: the microtask queue never empties
After N steps it yields to setTimeout
It throws RangeError like stack recursion
It is automatically turned into a macrotask

questions.text: MutationObserver callbacks are queued as microtasks.
Why can a Promise created inside setTimeout beat the next setTimeout, but not the current timer callback?
questions.answer: The current timeout is the macrotask already running. A promise from it enqueues a microtask, which runs right after that callback and before the next macrotask. The next setTimeout waits for a new macro turn, so the then runs first.
